# Final messages for measuring the Stop hook.
#
# Each case starts with a "=== <id>" line, then header lines:
#   expect: none | handback | own-work | readability (comma-separated)
#   user:   one of the user's messages (repeat the line for several, oldest first)
# then a line with "---", then the final assistant message up to the next "===".
# Lines starting with "#" before the first case are comments.
#
# "good" cases are messages the hook must leave alone. "bad" cases are the
# patterns it exists to catch. test_corpus.py runs every case through
# evaluate() and reports how often each check fires on each group.
# Cases with "holdout" in the id were written after the thresholds had been
# tuned on the others, to estimate how the hook does on messages it has not
# been fitted to.

=== good-answer-why-ci-slow
expect: none
user: Why is npm install so slow in CI? It takes 4 minutes every run.
---
Most of the install time goes to downloading packages, because the CI cache never hits.

The cache key in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is built from the commit SHA, so every new commit misses the cache and downloads all 1,400 packages again. That download is about 3 of the 4 minutes. With a warm cache the same install took 41 seconds on my machine.

Keying the cache on `package-lock.json` instead would let most runs reuse it. I haven't changed the workflow because you only asked why.

=== good-report-login-timeout
expect: none
user: Fix the login timeout bug. People get logged out after a few seconds of idle time.
---
The login timeout is fixed. Sessions were ending early because `refreshToken()` compared seconds with milliseconds, so a one hour session expired after about four seconds of idle time.

What changed:

- `src/auth/session.ts` now converts both values to milliseconds before comparing.
- `src/auth/session.test.ts` has a new test that idles for five seconds and stays logged in.
- `docs/auth.md` says which unit the setting uses.

I ran the whole test suite, which passes, and logged in on the local server and waited ten minutes without being logged out. I did not test the mobile app because it uses a separate login service that this change does not touch.

Nothing is left open. I kept the setting name the same so existing config files still work.

=== good-plan-user-asked
expect: none
user: Make a plan for moving the auth service from MySQL to Postgres. Don't change any code yet.
---
Here is the plan. It moves the data first and switches reads last, so we can roll back at every step.

1. Add a Postgres schema that mirrors the three auth tables, using the same column names.
2. Write a copy job that moves users, sessions and tokens in batches of 5,000 and checks row counts.
3. Dual-write new sessions to both databases for a week.
4. Switch reads to Postgres behind a feature flag, starting with 5% of logins.
5. Remove the MySQL code once the flag has been at 100% for a week with no errors.

The riskiest step is the token table, because it has 40 million rows and a unique index that MySQL treats case-insensitively. I'd start with step 1. Shall I start with step 1?

=== good-explain-question-then-offer
expect: none
user: How does the job scheduler decide which worker gets a job?
---
Each job goes to the worker with the fewest jobs in flight, and ties go to the worker that has been idle longest.

The scheduler keeps a count per worker that goes up when it hands out a job and down when the worker reports back. When a new job arrives it picks the lowest count. If a worker misses three heartbeats in a row, its count is treated as infinite, so it gets nothing until it reports in again.

Jobs with a "region" label skip this and go only to workers in that region, picked the same way.

If you want, I can walk through the code that does the picking.

=== good-code-block-answer
expect: none
user: How do I run a single test with pytest?
---
Give pytest the file and the test name, or use -k with part of the name:

```bash
pytest tests/test_api.py::test_login -q
pytest -k login
```

The first form runs exactly one test. The second runs every test whose name contains "login", which is handy when you don't remember the file.

=== good-long-conceptual-answer
expect: none
user: Explain why our Postgres queries got slower after the upgrade.
---
The queries got slower because the upgrade reset the planner statistics, so Postgres is guessing table sizes and picking poor plans. After a major upgrade the statistics are not carried over, and until the next ANALYZE the planner assumes every table is small. For small tables a sequential scan is the cheapest plan, so it scans the 30-million-row orders table from start to end instead of using the index on customer_id. That is why the order history page went from about 40 ms to over 6 seconds, while queries on small tables did not change at all.

You can see this in the query plan: it estimates 1,000 rows for the orders table and finds 30 million. Running ANALYZE on the database fixes it, and it takes about two minutes here. I ran it on the staging copy and the order history query went back to 38 ms.

I have not run it on production, because it adds load while it runs and you may want to pick the time.

=== good-medium-first-sentence
expect: none
user: Why does the nightly export fail on the first of the month?
---
The nightly export fails on the first of the month because the job asks for "yesterday's" partition by subtracting one from the day number, which gives day zero on the first, and the database rejects a date with day zero.

The fix is to subtract one day from the full date instead, which correctly rolls back to the last day of the previous month. I changed that in the export job and added a test that runs it with the date set to March 1st and January 1st.

All export tests pass. I also ran the job by hand for 1 March on the staging data, and it exported the 28 February partition as expected.

=== good-semicolons-two
expect: none
user: Summarise what you changed in the build.
---
The build is about 40% faster now. Three changes did most of it: the test step runs in four parallel shards; the Docker layers are cached between runs; and the lint step only looks at changed files.

A full build took 11 minutes before and takes 6 minutes 40 seconds now, measured over the last ten runs on the main branch. Nothing changed in what the build checks, so a failing test still fails the build the same way.

The one thing to watch is the shard count. If the test suite grows a lot, four shards may stop being enough, and the setting is at the top of the workflow file.

=== good-spanish-answer
expect: none
user: ¿Por qué falla el build en Windows?
---
El build falla en Windows porque el script de copia usa rutas con barras normales y `cp`, que no existe en cmd.

El paso concreto es `npm run copy-assets`, definido en package.json. En Linux y macOS funciona; en Windows termina con "cp no se reconoce como un comando interno".

Cambiarlo por el paquete cpy-cli lo arreglaría en los tres sistemas. No he cambiado nada porque solo preguntaste por qué falla.

=== good-chinese-answer
expect: none
user: 为什么首页加载这么慢？
---
首页慢主要是因为首屏一次加载了 3.2 MB 的图片，而且都没有压缩。

最大的三张轮播图每张约 900 KB，占了加载时间的大部分。在模拟 4G 网络下，首页完全加载需要 7.8 秒，去掉这三张图后只需要 2.1 秒。

把图片转换成 WebP 并按屏幕尺寸加载，可以把这部分降到 300 KB 左右。我还没有改代码，因为你只问了原因。

=== good-commit-hash-in-prose
expect: none
user: When did the search results start showing duplicates?

=== good-rhetorical-question-inside
expect: none
user: Why does the cron job only fail on Mondays?
---
So why only Mondays? Because the job runs at midnight UTC, which is Sunday evening in your timezone, and the weekly report table is locked by the Sunday backup until about 00:20 UTC.

On the other days the backup is not running, so the job gets the lock straight away. Moving the job to 01:00 UTC, or making the backup finish earlier, would stop the failures.

=== good-long-run-report
expect: none
user: Get the import job under 10 minutes for the full dataset. It takes 47 minutes now.
---
The full import now takes 8 minutes 20 seconds, down from 47 minutes.

Almost all of the time was spent inserting rows one at a time. The job now inserts them in batches of 2,000 and builds the search index once at the end instead of after every row. Those two changes account for 37 of the 39 minutes saved. The rest came from reading the input file in larger chunks.

I measured each change on the full 6.2-million-row file, three runs each, and kept only changes that made it faster. The imported data matches the old job exactly: same row count and the same checksum per table.

Two things are open. The job now needs about 1.5 GB of memory at its peak, up from 400 MB, which fits the current server but is worth knowing. And I left the old row-by-row code path behind a flag for one release, in case something unexpected shows up; it can be deleted after that.

=== bad-readability-dense-opening
expect: readability
user: Why are new worktrees so slow to set up on this machine?
---
Root cause is store-side, not git: `worktree add` is ~0.4 s; the tail is pnpm's per-tree link phase, with `node-linker=isolated` and the CAS under `~/.local/share/pnpm/store/v10`, the ~212k-inode hardlink fan-out falls back to copy since wt-3 is on a different mount (EXDEV), so reflink is ineligible; compounded by side-effects-cache misses from the postinstall hash drift seen in r7.

I changed the store location so it sits on the same disk as the worktrees, which lets pnpm hard-link files instead of copying them. A new worktree now installs in 14 seconds instead of 3 minutes.

I checked it by creating three fresh worktrees and timing each install. I did not change anything in the git setup, because git itself was already fast.

I changed the cache key so it includes the locale, which stops French pages from being served to English visitors. The fix is in the page cache module and nowhere else.

I checked it by running the full test suite, which passes, and by loading the home page in both languages on the local server. I did not test the CDN layer because it is not running here.

=== bad-readability-wall-opening
expect: readability
user: Make the build pass on every platform.
---
The build now passes on Linux, macOS and Windows, and getting there took changes in several places that all interacted with each other in ways that were not obvious at first, starting with the path handling in the asset copy step, which assumed forward slashes and broke on Windows, then the shell scripts that the test step called, which used GNU-only flags for sed and date and failed on macOS, then the line-ending settings in the repository, which made the snapshot tests fail on Windows because the stored snapshots had LF endings and the generated output had CRLF endings, and finally the native module build, which needed a newer compiler on the macOS runner than the default one, so I pinned the runner image and added a step that selects the right compiler version before the native build runs, and after all of that the whole matrix passes on three consecutive runs.

I checked it by running the full matrix three times on the main branch. I did not test on ARM Windows, because the CI provider doesn't offer it.

=== bad-readability-long-first-sentence
expect: readability
user: Why does the nightly sync miss some records?
---
The nightly sync misses records that are updated while it is running, because it reads the change log in pages ordered by update time and a record that is updated after its page was read but before the sync finishes moves to a later page that the sync has already decided not to read since it computed the total page count at the start, so those records wait for the next night and sometimes get skipped again if they keep changing.

Reading the change log by a fixed snapshot time instead of live update times would fix it. I tested that approach on a copy of last night's data and it picked up all 312 records that the current sync missed.

I haven't changed the production job yet because it runs in an hour and I didn't want to change it mid-cycle.

I moved the store onto the same disk as the worktrees, so a new worktree installs in 14 seconds instead of 3 minutes. I checked it by creating three fresh worktrees and timing each install.

Want me to add a check to the setup script that warns when the store is on a different disk?

=== good-holdout-cli-flags-answer
expect: none
user: What flags does the cleanup script take?
---
The cleanup script takes four flags. Use --dry-run to list what would be deleted, --older-than with a number of days to set the cutoff (30 by default), --force to skip the confirmation prompt, and --verbose to print each file as it goes.

A safe first run is --dry-run with your cutoff, then the same command without --dry-run once the list looks right.

=== good-holdout-why-with-numbers
expect: none
user: Why did the AWS bill jump last month?
---
The bill went up by $1,840, and $1,610 of that is data transfer out of the image bucket.

On 4 October the CDN in front of the bucket was removed when the old load balancer was deleted, so every image request since then has been served straight from the bucket at full transfer price. The daily transfer cost went from about $6 to about $58 that same day, and nothing else in the bill moved by more than $40.

Putting the CDN back in front of the bucket should bring it back down. I haven't changed anything in the account.

=== good-holdout-semicolon-inline-code
expect: none
user: Why does the config parser choke on the new line?
---
The parser splits each line on semicolons, and the new line has a semicolon inside a quoted value: `TITLE="Q4; final"`. The parser treats it as two settings and fails on the second half.

The fix is to split only on semicolons outside quotes. I made that change and added a test with the exact line from your config, and it now loads as one setting. The other 140 lines in the file load the same as before.

=== good-holdout-yaml-block-answer
expect: none
user: How do I make the CI job run only on the main branch?
---
Add a branch filter to the trigger at the top of the workflow file:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
```

Pull requests will then stop running it. If you still want it on pull requests that target main, add `pull_request: { branches: [main] }` next to the push trigger.

=== good-holdout-explain-tradeoff
expect: none
user: Should we use server-side rendering for the marketing site?
---
Yes, for the marketing site server-side rendering is the better choice, mainly because search engines and link previews see the full page straight away.

The pages change rarely and have no logged-in state, so they can be rendered once at build time and served as plain files. That gives the speed of a static site with full HTML for crawlers. The cost is a rebuild when content changes, which takes about a minute with the current page count.

Client-side rendering would only win if the pages became highly personalised, which is not the case today.

=== good-holdout-python-traceback-explain
expect: none
user: What does this error mean? KeyError: 'region' in loader.py
---
It means the config file being loaded has no "region" setting, and the loader reads it without a fallback.

The loader looks it up directly in load_settings(), so a missing key stops everything with that error. The sample config in the repo has the setting, but the one in your home folder was created before it was added last month.

Adding a "region" line to your config fixes it. A fallback to the default region in the loader would also stop the error for anyone else with an old config.

=== good-holdout-camelcase-names

---
The profile page re-renders on every keystroke because the form state lives at the top of the page, so each change re-renders every section, including the heavy activity chart.

Moving the form state into the form component and wrapping the chart in a memo stops that. After the change, typing in the name field re-renders only the form, and the chart renders once on load. I measured it with the React profiler: a keystroke went from 38 ms to 3 ms.

All component tests pass, and the profile still saves the same way.

=== good-holdout-sql-explain
expect: none
user: Why is the monthly report query slow?
---
The monthly report query is slow because it filters on the created date with a function, so Postgres can't use the index on that column and scans all 18 million orders.

The filter wraps the date in date_trunc, which hides the column from the index. Comparing the raw column with the first and last day of the month instead gives the same rows and lets the index work. On the staging copy that brought the query from 14 seconds to 120 ms, with identical results.

I haven't changed the report yet because you only asked why.

=== good-holdout-mixed-list-and-prose
expect: none
user: Migrate the project from npm to pnpm.
---
The project now uses pnpm. Installs take 22 seconds instead of 70, and the lock file is about a third of the size.

Three things needed changes beyond swapping the lock file:

- Two packages relied on undeclared dependencies, which pnpm doesn't allow, so I added those dependencies explicitly.
- The CI workflow caches the pnpm store instead of node_modules.
- The Docker build installs pnpm through corepack.

The full test suite passes locally and in CI, and the Docker image builds and starts. Anyone with an old node_modules folder should delete it once before the first pnpm install.

=== good-holdout-recommendation
expect: none
user: Pick an email provider for the transactional emails.
---
I'd use Postmark for the transactional emails, and I've set the app up with it.

It had the best delivery in the tests I could run here: all 50 test emails reached the inbox in under 10 seconds, against 47 for SES and 49 for SendGrid. It's also the simplest to set up for this kind of email only, and at your volume of about 20,000 emails a month it costs $15.

Switching later is a settings change, because the app sends through a small wrapper and not the provider's library directly. You'll need to verify the sending domain in Postmark before it works in production.

=== good-holdout-long-german-answer
expect: none
user: Warum ist der Build so langsam geworden?
---
Der Build ist langsamer geworden, weil seit dem letzten Update alle Bilder bei jedem Build neu komprimiert werden.

Früher lag ein Cache für die komprimierten Bilder im Build-Ordner. Das neue Update löscht diesen Ordner vor jedem Build, also werden alle 2.300 Bilder jedes Mal neu verarbeitet. Das allein dauert etwa sechs der acht Minuten.

Wenn der Cache in einen eigenen Ordner außerhalb des Build-Ordners verschoben wird, bleibt er erhalten. Ich habe das lokal ausprobiert: Der Build dauert damit wieder knapp zwei Minuten. Geändert habe ich noch nichts, weil du nur nach dem Grund gefragt hast.

=== bad-holdout-readability-jargon
expect: readability
user: Why does the app freeze when uploading big files?
---
Main-thread stall: `FileReader.readAsArrayBuffer()` on the 1.2 GB blob materialises it in the JS heap; `crypto.subtle.digest()` then hashes it synchronously w.r.t. the event loop's microtask drain; meanwhile `UploadQueue.flush()` holds the IDB txn open, so `onprogress` never fires and the UI looks frozen.

I changed the upload to read and hash the file in 8 MB pieces and to report progress after each piece. A 1.2 GB upload now shows steady progress and the page stays responsive the whole time.

I tested it with files of 100 MB, 1.2 GB and 4 GB in Chrome and Firefox. Safari still freezes briefly at the start of very large uploads, which I couldn't fix from the app side.

=== bad-holdout-readability-semicolon-bullets
expect: readability
user: What did you change in the deploy script?
---
The deploy script is faster and safer now.

- Builds: cached per commit; skipped when nothing changed; pruned after a week; logged to the deploy channel.
- Rollback: one command now; it restores the previous release and the previous config.
- Health checks: run after each server instead of at the end.

I ran a deploy and a rollback on staging and both worked. A deploy with no changes now takes 40 seconds instead of 6 minutes.
